## Introduction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) is proving to be a more and more powerful tool, and some people think that it is utterly inscrutable. 
However, I want to push back against that idea by teaching you about neural networks! 
Neural networks are the foundation of deep learning, so an understanding of neural networks can improve our understanding of AI!
In this blog, I aim to teach the fundamentals of the structure of neural networks, how they're trained, and give an example of neural networks in action.

## Basic Structure

The big picture of a neural network is to iteratively create a function that maps existing input x's onto correct output y's such that we can accurately predict y's given new x's.

### Neurons

![A basic neural network](images/Colored_neural_network.webp)

A neural network consists of a series of neurons (also called nodes) arranged in multiple interconnected layers that progress from an input layer, through "hidden layers," and end up in an output layer (as shown in the above image).
A given neuron works by:

1. taking all of the previous inputs (`x1` through `xn`), 
2. multiplying them by a weight (`w1` through `wn`), 
3. summing them (we'll call this sum `z`),
4. adding a "bias" to `z` (we'll call the bias `b`),
5. then passing it through a nonlinearity function (we'll call this sigma, but more on that later) .

With all of that together, the math for a given neuron's activation `a` will look like this: (Note that `z` looks remarkably similar to a linear regression equation.)
$$
z = w_1x_1 + w_2x_2+...+w_nx_n+b,\space\space a=\sigma(z)
$$

The reason we pass `z` into a nonlinearity function to get the neuron's activation is because introducing nonlinearity allows the neuron a greater measure of flexibility.
If not for our nonlinearity function, a given neuron would only be able to produce a straight line, which would miss out on a lot of higher level details. 
However, since nonlinear functions already have a bit of bend to them, transformations can the model fit the shape of the data incredibly well!

![Example of nonlinearity in action](images/nonlinearity.webp)

Commonly used functions are this are ReLUs (which excludes negative values) and Sigmoids (which condenses inputs to be between 0 and 1)

### Layers in Neural Networks

A neural network functions by having every neuron in a given layer interact with every neuron in the next layer.
The first layer is called the "input layer," and will have a node for every input you pass into the neural network (inputs can range from various medical variables such as BMI and heart rate to pixels from an image).

From there, every input neuron will connect with every node in the next "hidden layer."
These consist of nodes that aim to discover high-dimensional connections about the data through each node's unique combination of weights and biases. 
Each neuron in the hidden layer apply weights to the previous nodes' activations, then sum them and add a bias.
Later on, the node's weights and bias will be tuned through training to more effectively recognize hidden connections within the data. 
From there, these nodes' activations will be passed into additional hidden layers until the final layer is reached.

![A neural network with multiple hidden layers](images/multiple_hidden_layers.png)

Finally, after all of the neurons in the hidden layers activate, the neural network will return a value in the output layer. 
Sometimes this value will manifest as a probability between which of multiple outcomes will most likely be observed, or as a single number that predicts some metric (such as life expectancy). 
This will give us the outputs that we'll test for accuracy in the training phase. 

## Training Process
### Analyzing Loss
Naturally, nobody will perfectly set up a neural network on the first try. 
However, you can optimize a neural network through a process called gradient descent, where you pay attention to the model's MSE (or some other loss function), then systematically adjust the linear combination of each node's weights in the direction that will reduce the MSE the most. 
After enough iterations, the loss should be significantly diminished!
$$
MSE = \text{mean}((w*x-y))^2
$$

### Training, Validation, and Testing
But how would one find the loss the equation for MSE requires the y to be known?
Well, a neural network only works after it's trained, so it requires a bunch of real data that has outputs mapped to inputs and models what the network will be testing.
To train the network properly, the data should be split into a training set, a validation set, and a test set.

The training set will help the network form its weights, the validation set will act as out-of-sample checkpoints that make sure the network is being trained properly, and the test set will be set aside until the very end of the training period to see how the model would perform on brand new data.

This method of training is vital to make sure that the model is capable of acting outside the current data it has been trained on. 
If the model only picks up on the high level connections within the data, it can become overfit and will not be as accurate with new data.
(Overfitting can also occur when there are too many hidden layers that get trained on small amounts of data.) 


## Example with MNIST Data
The MNIST database is a massive database that consists of tens of thousands of handwritten numbers in a 28x28 pixel resolution that each come with classifying labels.

![Example images from MNIST](/images/MNIST_dataset_example.png)

This dataset is a classic for explaining the process of how neural networks function.

Since there are 784 pixels in a given 28x28 image, one would initialize the neural network with 784 neurons in the input layer. 
Additionally, since there are 10 numbers that the number could be, the neural network will have 10 output neurons that correspond to 0-9.
The person setting up the neural network would also divide the data into a training, validation, and testing set, then would begin the training process.

Each input layer node will accept a number between 0.00 and 1.0 that represents the pixel's grayscale as that input neuron's activation.

![Example MNIST input with pixel activations](/images/MNIST_Input.png)

From there, those inputs will be passed into the first hidden layer (whose number of neurons will depend on how the neural network is set up, since there are lots of different advantages to different structures).
Then, each node from the first hidden layer will act as the input for the next hidden layer, which will continue until the output layer is reached.
The output layer node with the highest activation will be what the network classifies the number as.

From there, the neural network will figure out the MSE for all the output neurons compared to the real classifying label (which will be 0 for all outputs except the correct label), then do some gradient descent to adjust the weights, then will try another run-through with a different image from the training set.

Finally, after enough rounds of training and validation, the model will be run with the test set to see how accurate it is with brand new data.

Additionally, I hope that the parallels to AI is clear, between the fact that they are able to synthesize massive amounts of data to make predictions for future data, and how the way data is used to train a model can be massively impactful (such as when the Google AI got overfit on Reddit comments and gave terrible advice).
If you are interested in learning more, I'd strongly reccomend looking into supplementary training processes, such as learning rates, weight decay, dropout, or early stopping!
